questions.question: Why are subword tokenizers (like BPE) preferred over word-level tokenizers?
options: They handle unseen words by breaking them into smaller, known pieces.
They are much slower but more accurate.
They eliminate the need for any vocabulary at all.
questions.explanation: Word-level tokenizers fail on any word not in their fixed dictionary. Subword tokenizers can represent 'untokenizable' as 'un' + 'token' + 'izable', ensuring the model always has a signal.

questions.question: What does 'byte-level BPE' (used in GPT-2 and Llama) guarantee?
options: Zero [UNK] (unknown) tokens, as any string can be represented by its raw bytes.
That every word will be exactly one token.
That the model will run 10x faster.
That the model only understands 256 words.
questions.explanation: By starting with the 256 possible bytes rather than Unicode characters, the tokenizer can always fall back to individual bytes for any character it hasn't seen before.

questions.question: What is the main difference between BPE and Unigram tokenization?
options: BPE is a bottom-up merge approach; Unigram is a top-down probabilistic pruning approach.
BPE is only for characters; Unigram is only for words.
BPE requires a GPU; Unigram doesn't.
They are identical except for the library that implements them.
questions.explanation: BPE starts small and builds up by merging frequent pairs. Unigram starts with a huge set of candidates and prunes them down to maximize the likelihood of the training data.

questions.question: What is 'fertility' in tokenization?
options: The average number of tokens produced per word in a given language.
The number of new words a model can learn per day.
The number of languages supported by the tokenizer.
questions.explanation: High fertility is bad: it means the tokenizer is inefficient for that language, using many tokens to represent a single word, which shortens the effective context window.
